utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can the witness make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please sit down. Yes, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to all the parties. Good morning sir. My colleague, Krgovic will question Mr. Mihalj but at the beginning I would just like to ask the Chamber about the -- so we would like to -- we are talking about the redacted statements so what we would like to do is before we start to provide the Court with these edited statements, redacted statements, so that they could be given numbers. They have been completely redacted so is it the best thing to do to provide them now so that these redacted statements would then be available for the Chamber as well as the witness during questioning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, please, Mr. Ilija Mihalj will testify now. His statement already has an ID statement, D120/3 ID and now, according to the instructions of the Trial Chamber, we will present to the witness the redacted statements which had the relevant sections taken out. There is a version in English and in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Is there a copy for the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The interpreters were wondering whether they have a copy. They don't actually need one because the viva voce evidence will not be from the statement. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mihalj.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please put the statement down for the time being and if you could just turn your chair a little bit so that you would be sitting facing straight in front? Yes, that's right. Sir, could you please tell us your name?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: My name is Ilija Mihalj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in order to go through this proceedings as soon as possible, I will just read out the general information contained in this statement and if you could just confirm for me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We already have the particulars so there is no need to repeat them. You simply go straight to the evidence required.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mihalj, could you please tell us, did you sign this statement in Samac, the statement that is in front of you right now?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Yes, I signed this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the exhibit, full exhibit number for this statement, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We don't need to go through that. We already have these numbers, what the Registry will do is simply formally record them properly. And we already have the particulars of the witness so just go straight forward to the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mihalj, could you please tell us where did you live before the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Before the war, I lived in Odzak, in Bosanska Posavina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mihalj, could you please tell us, were you a member of any political party before the war?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: I wasn't a member of any party during the war, but afterwards, in peace time, I was a member of the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't get the name of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the name of this party that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: New Croatian Initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mihalj, could you please tell us, until when did you live in Odzak? Before the outbreak of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: I lived in Odzak until the last day, five to six days before the fall of Odzak. In the meantime, I returned, I went to Croatia and came back to Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When did you definitely leave Odzak?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: I left Odzak in the month of July. I don't remember the date, whether it was the 6th or the 7th. It was approximately around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: I went to Slavonski Brod in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: After a certain amount of time, did you return to Odzak?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: I returned to Odzak -- how do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: To live.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Again?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes, after the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mihalj, in your statement, you've already said that you know Mr. Tadic from before the war, that you were on good terms with him. I'm not going to ask you about those things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Don't repeat what has already been admitted, please. Let's go back to the evidence that was redacted. That's all you need to lead the witness on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You described in the previous paragraphs your preparations for departure and preparations to see Miroslav Tadic. When you arrived, could you please tell us where did you meet Miroslav Tadic then when you went to get his help about the exchange of Ivo Doslic whom you mentioned? Where was this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: The meeting took place in Dragalic. It's a settlement towards -- in the direction of Zagreb. I think it's about 70 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Was this -- could you please tell us whether this was in the UNPA zone under the control -- the zone under the control of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, when you went to this meeting with Tadic, did you go -- is that the place where the negotiations took place or the exchange took place?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: The negotiations took place on that day. There was no exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one moment, Your Honours, please, so that I can consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mihalj, could you please tell us who was present on that occasion from the Croatian side when you met with Miroslav Tadic?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Mijo Matanovic was there. I was there. There was a person from Gradiska, I don't know his name. He was the mayor of Gradiska later. I think the Red Cross was present and also the people from the United Nations who were taking care of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And who was there from the opposite side?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Mr. Miro Tadic was there from the opposite side. Grujicic, we called him Grujo. There was a lawyer from Doboj by the name of Lukic and there was another man, an older man, I don't know his name. He stood to the side a little bit further off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mihalj you said that you had prepared some money, that you wanted to offer to Tadic. Could you please tell me how did you come to the idea to offer this money to Tadic? Did you -- did you -- what was the reason for you to offer money? Did you hear something? What was your motive?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: The money was -- we have gotten used to in these transitional country of ours to offer that when we go for a drink or something so that was a reason, the reason why I took the money, the situation had changed but this was our habit in any kind of transaction, in the former Yugoslavia, to offer money.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mihalj, did you meet with Tadic on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Yes. I met Mr. Tadic near Dragalic where the talks were held, the negotiations were held, about the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you say hello to Tadic? Could you describe in a couple of sentences how this meeting between you proceeded?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: They prepared this document for me so that I could go through the UNPA zone so I had a pass from the police, also from the HVO and the Croatian Army so when I arrived, Miro was there. I stood there. I stopped close by in my car. And then when he saw me, we immediately started walking towards one another and he said, where are you coming from? And he [as interpreted] said well, I need to see you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you greet each other?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Yes, we greeted each other, we kissed, we hadn't seen each other for a long time. Just like we would usually do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour one small correction for the transcript on page 6, line 21, and I said, well, I need to see you. It's not and he said, well, I need to see you. This is what the witness said. He actually needed to see Mr. Tadic. He had something to discuss with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps that can be corrected with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mihalj, when you were describing this encounter of yours and this first contact with Tadic, can you please repeat what you said to Tadic? Because the way it's recorded in the transcript is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: It was a meeting, afterwards a couple of us sat down for a couple of minutes and I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your first contact, what you said about when Miroslav Tadic asked you where are you coming from, what did you respond to him?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: There is a detainee called Doslic in Samac so I'm here to see about this man, Ivo Doslic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Before you started this conversation, did you tell Tadic, "I've come to see you"?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, Mr. Mihalj, could you describe how you started the conversation about this Doslic and what did you offer Mr. Miroslav Tadic?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: I personally didn't know Doslic. I heard his name in a restaurant in a cafe, and this owner, Grozd asked me to go to Dragalic and to see. When we were sitting there, while they were over there, this, going through the script of the detained, me and Mr. Miro stood about a metre or so away from his car and I told him that I had brought some money, if this was necessary, so I could give that to him. It was about 5.000 German marks. And Miro said, "Ilija, I don't need the money. We don't take money. We have to try to help everybody and to have each ethnic group exchanged so that everybody could go to their home."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Just a small correction, excuse me, Mr. Mihalj, but in the transcript, on page 7, line 24, you said that the owner of the cafe called Grozd --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What was the name of the owner?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Anto Jukic. He was the one who gave me the money.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: One more correction. Page 8, lines 5 and 6, when you said that Tadic had replied, "I don't need the money," and everyone should be at home, every member of every ethnic group should go to his own home?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please sit a little closer to the microphone so that the interpreters can hear you properly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Krgovic, one thing in the transcript on line 25 of page 7, it says, "when we were sitting there, while they were over there, this, going through the script of the detained, me and Mr. Miro stood about a metre or so away from his car," I'm uncertain in terms of the translation, when we were sitting there, and they were over there, going through the script of the detained, I presume that means lists or something like that, but could you clarify the sitting here and there? Doesn't really seem to make too much sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mihalj, let's clarify this. You were sitting to one side with Miroslav Tadic apart from the others and you sat down somewhere?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Yes, it was two metres away from the car. This was at a petrol pump. The two of us were sitting together and talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And who was sitting beside you and looking at those lists?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Well, a little further away, those lists were on the car, and Grewo and the people from Gradiska [Realtime transcript read in error "grad I shall you"] were looking at them, the people who were in charge of those lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So the negotiators?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I wasn't interested in those lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that we need some corrections for the transcript. First of all, on page 9, line 9, first word is G-r-e-w-o. It's a name of a person Grujicic Milutin, nicknamed Grewo, who was before this Trial Chamber as a witness, if you remember. So just to have it clear for the transcript. And here in the same line, page 9, people from Gradiska, it's Gradiska. It's a name of town, Gradiska. So this means the representative of Gradiska. That's it. And now that's the -- this makes sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, let's proceed. Thank you for the corrections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mihalj, when you mentioned to Miroslav Tadic this man Doslic did he know anything about him?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: He knew nothing about him. We went to where the papers were and we found him on this script or list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you were looking for this in the script, who was leafing through it?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: They were all standing around the car, the man from Gradiska and Grujicic and I myself because they allowed me to, and Mr. Miro.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Mihalj, the name of Ivo Doslic was on the list of persons to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Yes, it was. And there were some marks next to his name indicating that he was to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did Grujicic say anything to you on that occasion about the possibility of having Doslic exchanged?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: He told me that he was supposed to come on Tuesday, and although I wanted to go and look around --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please limit your replies to my questions. We will come to these details later on. Just tell me what Grujicic told you?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: That Ivo was supposed to come on the following Tuesday. I don't know what day it was but on the following Tuesday he was supposed to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Was Ivo Doslic exchanged on the following Tuesday?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: I tried to find out and he wasn't. It was on the Tuesday after that, so they skipped a Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when he was exchanged, what month was it?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: It was September, I think. It was hot. We were lying there on the grass.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What year was it? Was it in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Yes, in 1992, it was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Mihalj, did you try to find out and were you told why Doslic was not exchanged on the following Tuesday but on the Tuesday after? Did Tadic send you a message about this?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Well, it was probably the institutions in charge of the exchanges and some documents could not be made ready in time for that Tuesday. The institutions in [Realtime transcript read in error "Naser Sejdic"] charge of that weren't able to do it on time so that's why he couldn't come on that Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, when you saw Tadic, did you ask him for anything else?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, page 11, line 7 says Naser Sejdic. Never this witness mentioned this name and it has nothing to do with all this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can you just be asked to repeat what he said slowly?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mihalj, we were having some technical problems with the transcript. So could you please, when you were talking about the reasons why this man was not exchanged on the following Tuesday, you mentioned the approval of various institutions. Could you repeat that answer?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: On the first Tuesday after the agreement, Ivo Doslic did not arrive because of some papers that other institutions were supposed to prepare in order for Doslic to be exchanged on that Tuesday. So that instead, he came on the Tuesday after that. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, unless I've missed something the witness has referred to the first Tuesday after the agreement. I haven't heard -- unless I've missed it, I haven't heard any evidence of an agreement or what it might be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said after the talks, but I will discuss it with the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, let's proceed slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let's proceed slowly. After what, after your meeting?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: After the meeting where there were negotiations, he was supposed to -- that is Ivo Doslic whom I don't even know was supposed to be exchanged on the following Tuesday but in fact he arrived 15 days later rather than seven days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't mention a man called Naser Sejdic?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: I don't know anyone called Naser. I know what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Mihalj, on that occasion, when talking to Tadic, did you ask him for anything else? Did you ask him to go to your house and bring you some things?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I did. Along with all the other things we talked about, I asked him to go to my house in Odzak and if he found photographs of my children, and some 15 or 20 days later or a month later he sent me those photographs. I can't be precise about the date but I received a plastic bag full of photographs from my house. Later on, -- yeah, he sent them to me by Mijo Matanovic who handed me those pictures in Djakovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to contact Tadic again before the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: No. We didn't talk by phone or anything, but we met after I returned to Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Mihalj, the money that you took along to give to Tadic, did you return it to that man?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Yes, as soon as I got into the car I gave the money back and I said that Miro didn't want to take the money. I gave Anto back his 5.000 marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And what did Anto say to you?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: He was surprised. He didn't say anything but he was surprised. I could have kept the money but I didn't want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What impression did Tadic leave on you then? Was he very firm when he rejected the money?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Yes. He said I don't need money, we are not doing this for money. Well, he could have taken it but that was his response.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You knew Tadic both before and after the war. What was his financial status?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Very good. Excellent. He was among the most prosperous people in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mihalj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. -- it is not the intention of the Trial Chamber to allow other counsel to ask the witnesses because these are matters that have already been covered so we will just have cross-examination from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, this is just what I wanted to ask for instructions, whether I'm entitled to ask any questions or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I see. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, on the -- because of this decision, I would like to ask about how to proceed, when the next counsel have their turn, there may be something that is detrimental to another Defence. I have already read some statements from the other Defence teams, if there is something mentioned that hinders my Defence will I be allowed to put questions to those witnesses in the interests of the defence of my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Unless you can show the Trial Chamber that that is the first time that that matter has been mentioned because most of these statements are actually discussing cumulative evidence so you have already cross-examined on the same issues, there is no need to repeat the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour. That's just what I thought. If we see something in a 92 bis statement that runs counter to our Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What I'm saying is unless that's the first time that that matter has been mentioned which the Trial Chamber does not believe will be the case, because almost all these statements are actually -- the evidence is cumulative. The viva voce witnesses have already covered almost everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Prosecution? MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, if Your Honours please, I have just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Anto Jukic wanted to get his friend, Doslic out of the secondary school prison in Bosanski Samac, correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did he raise the issue with you of doing something about it?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: He came to you and sought your assistance?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The reason that he came to you and sought your assistance was that you knew Tadic very well, you were friends with him?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Yes. He was my teacher, and we were on good terms since 1965 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The other reason that Anto Jukic came to you was that both of you knew that Tadic was the man who controlled the exchanges?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Jukic didn't know about Mr. Miroslav Tadic. Rather in the cafe, Mijo Matanovic said to him that Mr. Tadic was at the negotiations in Dragalic, and that was why I went there. They asked me to go, both Mijo Matanovic and Anto Jukic. And he was a relative of Anto Jukic's not a friend, if I may correct my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Very well. It was Mijo Matanovic who explained to you and Anto Jukic that Mr. Tadic was the man to see in order to get someone exchanged, correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And whose idea was it to get together the 5.000 deutschmarks to pay for this exchange?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: We all had the same idea. We were used to it. It's hard to say who mentioned it first. We put it in our pockets and set out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And you were aware, weren't you, that by September of 1992, the exchanges had been going on for some months and that Mr. Tadic had been involved in those exchanges for some months in that area?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I interrupted you. Please finish your answer.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: But I saw him on that occasion only, but I did hear that he was taking part in exchanges and negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mijo Matanovic was, as far as you could tell, a man who had also considerable experience in the arrangement of exchanges?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Mijo was on the Croatian side. I didn't know very much about the exchanges, but Mijo was in charge on the Croatian side, our side.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: He was obviously -- knew a lot more about the system of exchanges, how it worked, who the important personalities were, compared to you and Anto Jukic?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. The result of your discussions is that you three considered that a bribe was necessary, or might be necessary, to arrange this exchange?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Well, as I said, this was the custom in the former Yugoslavia, to give bribes, but on this occasion, it was not successful, and Miro refused it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Customary or not, it was a bribe, plain and simple, wasn't it? You were planning to pay a bribe?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Yes. We were planning to do that but we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And furthermore, 5.000 deutschmarks in 1992 was a lot of money, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: 5.000 deutschmarks was always a lot of money.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Particularly --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: But, well, it depends on the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. I suppose it does. But as far as you three were concerned, it was a lot of money, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Yes. It was a lot of money, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And with this 5.000 dollars -- sorry, 5.000 deutschmarks, you considered it appropriate when you actually met Mr. Tadic, to offer the money?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: We didn't consider it to be a lot of money but in the war we kind of lost our bearings. We thought well the times have changed, we didn't know what was going on in Bosanska Posavina and they didn't know what was going on in Croatia, so -- that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. When you met Mr. Tadic at the exchange, you decided to offer and did in fact offer the 5.000 deutschmarks to him, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Yes. I was sitting with him near his car, and I said that I brought it for him to try and Miro said that the money was not necessary that we would see when Doslic was meant to be in the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And the reason that you offered the money was that you, Mijo Matanovic and Anto Jukic had all concluded that in order to get Doslic exchanged you had to in fact pay a bribe to Mr. Tadic, correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Yes. Just one correction, Mr. Prosecutor. Mijo Matanovic didn't know anything about these Deutsche German marks, only myself and Anto Jukic knew about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mihalj I will ask you several questions now regarding the questions asked by the Prosecutor and the answers that you gave to the Prosecutor. The Prosecutor suggested that you should answer to his questions that he was the one who was in control of the exchanges and he was the person who was in charge regarding the exchanges.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You were at this place where the negotiations were taking place. Who was the chief there? Who was the main person in charge for the negotiations? Who was Miroslav Tadic's chief?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: We didn't know if Miro was in charge. We had only heard that he took part in these exchanges. Grujicic was the chief. And from the other side this person from Gradiska, even Mijo -- Mijo and Miro were not in charge. I don't know what the name is of this person from Gradiska. I wasn't even interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, did Tadic tell you that he was in charge, that he was deciding?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: No, no. He didn't say anything like that. We just based ourselves on the issue of Doslic and we just stuck to seeing when he was meant to be in the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So who told you that he would be exchanged on Tuesday? Was that Tadic or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: They opened up a book and we all looked in this book and he said that on Tuesday, Doslic was supposed to be exchanged. When we were all looking in the book we looked in the -- and it was listed in alphabetical order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But who had this book?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Grujicic had the book. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, none of this arose in cross-examination. It's all stuff that could have been covered in chief. I didn't ask anything about the actual negotiations themselves other than the question of the offer of money.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: There was a question about who was in charge of the exchanges. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, very well. I'll withdraw my objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mihalj, based on these conversations with the people and with Tadic and with Grujicic, what was your impression? Who was in charge of these exchanges?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MIHALJ
utterances.text: Grujicic was in charge. This is what we heard and this is what we read about. Grujicic was in charge. He had all the papers. Miro and I were a bit too -- a bit off to the side, two or three metres from the car. And that's where we talked to Grujicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mihalj. Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mihalj, for giving evidence to the Tribunal. We have finished. You may go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, may I just cross the bar table and confer with my colleague, Mr. Lukic for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, you can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very well, the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber is informed that there is no witness waiting. What has happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I informed the service yesterday that three witnesses should be ready today and possibly a fourth one. This is what I informed the witness and victims protection unit. The next witness is to be Zeljko Volasevic, even though I didn't specify the timings. Mr. Mihalj was planned for less than an hour for the examination-in-chief and then the cross. Perhaps this is happening because the cross-examination of Mr. Mihalj took a little more than five minutes. Perhaps the witnesses are still at the hotel. Perhaps we can take a break early but in any event we do have three witnesses ready for today and possibly the fourth. While we are waiting, perhaps I can hand you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... two besides this one. It's strange that they just brought one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I asked for all three witnesses to be here at 9.00 in the morning to be here and to wait. Our practice is to have the witnesses brought altogether. We've had witnesses who have been here sitting and waiting all day. That's been our practice to date. While we are waiting, I can hand over the redacted statements of Zeljko Volasevic, they are ready. This is the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: In fact we can have all of them, if you have them, so... Yes. We understand some witnesses are just coming up so we can have those statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've just seen that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can the witness make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please sit down. Yes, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here are the redacted statements for the witness and for the Chamber. The witness is Mr. Volasevic. The rest of the statements I can -- they are all ready and I can hand them over during the next break. According to the decision of the Trial Chamber, the Defence will not be questioning this witness but he will be

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: preliminary question of the witness or will you ask the Prosecution to begin with the cross-examination right away?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Because you have already prepared him, that he's going to be cross-examined on the evidence which he gave in his statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. Then we simply go ahead with cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I can ask the witness only whether he signed the statement, if this would be of use to you, but he did sign the statement so, if -- I don't need to ask it, then perhaps we could move to the cross-examination straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we can simply move to the cross-examination. Yes, the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, are any of the other Defence counsel planning to cross the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. No, the Trial Chamber will only allow questions by other counsel if there is something completely knew. They are not going to cross-examine on the same issues that have been discussed with the other four viva voce witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Volasevic. My name is Phillip Weiner. I'm with the Office of the Prosecutor and I'm going to be asking you some questions this morning. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Thank you and good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, you served in the local commune in Bosanski Samac for some 15 years, isn't that correct? Or you served in the local commune for many years?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Over some 15 years you served as its secretary?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And as its secretary, you were responsible for maintaining the electoral rolls for the community of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And by the electoral rolls, you mean the voting lists?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now these voting lists were the ones that were used in the municipal elections in 1990, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What were these voting lists used for then?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: For elections in the local unit or as we call it the local commune, and only for the territory of the local commune, numbering approximately 6.000 citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you were aware of the election in 1990, the municipal election, where many people from the local commune or from the town of Bosanski Samac voted?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you recall that it was a very large turnout, over 80 per cent came and voted?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And a 50 person assembly was elected as a result of that elections?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that assembly included members of the HDZ party, the SDA and SDS?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And another two parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, some smaller parties.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: The SDP and the reform forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, after April 17th, 1992, this elected assembly or this democratically elected assembly, was no longer in power, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: There was now a Serbian Municipality of Samac and Pelagicevo under formation that had taken power, that was the name of the new city?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And instead of the elected, the democratically elected government, there was now a Crisis Staff that was in charge of this Serbian municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes but at the level of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. And you were aware that Blagoje Simic was president, the defendant Blagoje Simic was president of that Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you're aware that there were no HDZ or SDA members in that Crisis Staff of the Serbian Municipality of Bosanski Samac and Pelagicevo under formation?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but a little later, because this was municipal policy, while I conducted only affairs only at the level of the local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that. I'm just going through some of the new changes that occurred after April 17th in the municipality. And do you also agree that with this Crisis Staff, the elected assembly was no longer in existence? In fact some of its members were being imprisoned?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, are you saying that the assembly that was elected in 1990 was still in existence even though there was a new municipality -- a new Serbian municipality and a new Serbian Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I must again rest on that. These were bodies at the municipal level so I'm not familiar with the criteria based on which the municipal assembly was elected but I do know the criteria for the election in the municipal commune. I am aware of the regulations governing that. The other level is something that some other people were responsible for so I'm not informed about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. And you know, because you're familiar with the election, that the Crisis Staff and the Serbian assembly were not in office pursuant to a popular election of Samac residents. You're aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: The municipality of Bosanski Samac had 26 local communes where elections were held so I am really not informed about how the elections proceeded in those local communes which parties won there and I don't know at what level the municipal assembly is elected. The only thing that I know is the level at which the assembly of the local commune is elected as well as its bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir. I understand that but the question was: The Serbian Crisis Staff that took power after April 17th was not elected by the people in the municipality of Samac or by the people in your local commune. They didn't hold a public election and elect and install that Serbian Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that with this question, they are trying to confuse the witness. I think the proper way would be to ask the witness does he know how the Crisis Staff was elected? Does he know who was in the municipality, in the Assembly of the Serbian People, and then ask him whether this body was elected in such a way. Can he say who was in the Crisis Staff and who was in the assembly of the Serbian people of the municipality of Samac? That would be the first step.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour I was going to get to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: In addition, Mr. Weiner, the witness I think has explained almost three times which level of elections he was dealing with and what he knows, what level of knowledge he has as to the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: However, I think I have the right to ask him if he's aware that any special election was held where a Crisis Staff was elected in Samac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Asking him directly rather than putting statements to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware of any election in Samac where the Crisis Staff was elected prior -- the Serbian Crisis Staff was elected prior to April 17th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you know when this Serbian Municipality of Samac and Pelagicevo under formation was established?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Not officially, but in the town, talking to my neighbours, I learned that it had been established but I don't know where or how or by whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you had at least learned that it had been established prior to April 17th?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you sir. Were you aware that it had been established in February of 1992? Or sometime prior to April 17th?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you indicated in your statement that the local commune, at the local commune, sometime in the spring of 1992, they had some weapons, a rifle, a pistol, and you had a telephone to call police or other authorities in case of an emergency. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What were you planning to do with these weapons, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: I personally wasn't planning to do anything but the coordinating body said that for our personal safety, because we had organised night duty in case we had to intervene, for the personal security of those on duty, we were given a rifle and a pistol. These were locked up during the day and in the evening they were given to the person on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you said in case you have to intervene. Intervene against what or whom?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say intervene. I said for our personal defence, should there be some sort of incident that might threaten the lives of those people at night, because there were criminals and all sorts of people in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, were these weapons ever used? Any of these weapons ever used, before or after April 17th?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you were aware on or about April 17th, 1992, that Serbian volunteers and that Serbian police from outside of the municipality, were taking over all of the vital buildings and facilities in Samac, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the first part of your question? It wasn't clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sure, sir. Were you aware that the Serbian volunteers, those who you said spoke in the Ekavian dialect, whom you didn't know, they were from outside of Bosnia, had come into Samac, were taking over buildings, vital facilities, taking over the town? You were aware of that, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but only on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you were also aware that a new Crisis Staff had been installed on or about that date?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: On the 17th and the 18th, I didn't know that. I heard it only after the 20th, that there was some sort of Crisis Staff in the municipality. Before the civilian protection staff was to be set up. I don't remember the exact day when this was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you take any action to remove -- did you or members of the local commune take any action to remove these Serbian volunteers or to reinstate the democratically elected government of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: I personally wasn't able to. I was simply a technical person preparing materials, agreeing on the dates of the sessions, with the others. But whether the coordinating body tried to do something with the Crisis Staff, I don't know. I didn't take part in any of those meetings or talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you're not aware of the local commune taking any action to remove this Crisis Staff and to reinstate the democratically elected government? You're not aware of any action, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not aware of anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, in fact, you indicate on the morning of the 18th or the 17th or 18th, you see some men, a handful of Muslims, with rifles. You indicated that in your statement, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You don't mention in your statement that the town was being taken over or the town was taken over, isn't that correct? You never mention that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: I don't mention it because the night before, I attended a meeting at the local commune, I went home, went to sleep in the morning I was awakened by the people on duty. I went to replace him --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The question was, you don't mention in your statement that the town was taken over. You don't mention that, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You knew that a few days later. You don't mention that a few days later, that you learned that the town was taken over?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't feel it necessary to mention it because that's well known from other statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You don't mention in your statement that Serbian police and Serbian volunteers were taking over and controlling the vital buildings and facilities within the town. You don't mention that in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This line of questioning, Your Honours, is confusing the witness. The question should be whether the witness saw Serbian volunteers, whether he saw police, at facilities, whether he knows that power was taken over, and then these questions can be put to him. This sort of direct question is aimed at confusing the witness rather than establishing the facts. I can clarify this when it's my turn to re-examine but the facts should be established first.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, he's listed six or seven pages of facts in his statement. Those facts have been accepted as an exhibit. I am questioning what he -- I am questioning him about the facts that he has in that statement and on the issue of bias questioning him as to the facts that he has not placed in that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You ask him whether he knows what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I've asked him that previously. He's indicated that the Serb police and paramilitaries took over the vital buildings and he learned that on or about April 20th. And now I'm saying to him, a little bit later, you never mention that in your statement, you never mentioned the takeover in your statement and I have a few other questions I'm going to ask him why he didn't -- or that indicate that he has not mentioned those in his statement. Those are significant facts that occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. You see, Mr. Weiner, the point is this witness stated the things that are in his statement according to the way he's -- the Defence counsel prepared him. What issues they wanted him to discuss. So you simply ask him whether he knows that those events happened, how they happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, however, Your Honour, these are very important and significant events which occurred in Samac. How can you talk about what happened in Samac without talking about a takeover and I would argue the fact that he doesn't mention that there was a Serbian takeover is a question as to his bias and credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. The Trial Chamber does not agree. You simply ask him whether he knows what transpired and who did what and if he says so then you put it to him that he never mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Because if I may add then you're assuming that every individual in that area of Bosanski Samac knew exactly what was going on regarding the events of the 16th, 17th, who did what, which cannot be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The fact that he knew that these things happened but didn't mention them, I feel goes to his credibility or bias and these are the most significant facts that occurred during that four day period. He -- in his statement he has no problem talking about I saw Muslim and Croats running through the backyards. I saw Muslims trying to hold a meeting. I saw Muslims trying to do this but does he mention that armed paramilitaries are taking over the town? No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ask him whether he saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It's right in his statement, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That he saw the paramilitaries taking over?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No. He doesn't include that. He has no problems saying that he saw the Muslims and Croats in the town. If you look at his statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner we already looked at his statement. What I'm saying is he describes what he saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So ask him whether he saw those other people you want him to discuss.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The fact that he leaves out any other information which you feel he should put in his statement doesn't necessarily mean that he's biased.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour as you know if a defendant or if a Prosecutor does not call certain witnesses, does not refer to certain witnesses, does not refer to certain tests being done either party can argue that it was done for certain reasons and as a result it should affect their case. The failure to call a certain witness does have an effect, whether it's on bias, whether it's on credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That is a different issue. Here we are discussing what this witness knows, what he stated in his statement, and you can cross-examine him. Ask him what he knows, whom he saw. He has stated the people he saw. Maybe because they were near where he was placed. You ask him how he saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you saw Serbian paramilitaries, whether you want to call them volunteers or paramilitaries in the town, those people in the camouflage uniforms speaking in an Ekavian dialect. They even came to your home, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't see them. Had I known that the Serbian forces were taking over the town, perhaps I wouldn't have taken my children out. I said in my statement I wasn't aware of that until the following afternoon. It was then that I learned what had happened in the town exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's what I'm asking you about. I'm not asking you strictly about the 17th, the 17th, 18th, 19th, 20th, the first week, you became aware and you saw Serbian paramilitaries in the town and they came to your home too, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes but that was on the third day approximately, when weapons were being collected and they didn't enter the houses, they used a loud speaker to call on citizens regardless of their ethnicity, who had weapons, to hand them in. There were all three ethnic groups in my street and we all took out what weapons we had. They didn't enter the houses or mistreat or touch anyone. I could have not taken my weapons out. That was the first time I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you weren't aware that the Serbian paramilitaries had entered homes and were mistreating people during the first week after the 17th?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You weren't aware that Serbian paramilitaries had entered a home had arrested Izetbegovic and mistreated him, tortured him and even extracted some of his teeth? You weren't aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You weren't aware that the president of the SDA, Sulejman Tihic, was arrested, beaten, beaten at the police station by Serbian paramilitaries? You weren't aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Not in those first days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you became aware of that later, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: I learned that they had been arrested, but that they had been mistreated, I don't know whether this is true or not. I heard that only a year later when I had already left Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, having worked for many years with electoral rolls and in elections, were you appalled or confused by what you were learning over that next week about a takeover in Samac, about a government, a Serbian Crisis Staff, appointing itself to be in control of the city? Were you appalled by that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am confused by this question because I think several facts are mentioned in the question, that the Crisis Staff appointed itself, took over control, and in the first part of the question, what is the connection with his work on electoral rolls and elections? Could this be put more clearly and each part separately?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner, can you break up your question and also please remember that the witness did talk about getting involved in elections at the local commune level.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you were involved for many years in electoral rolls and in elections, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Having spent many years involved in democratic style elections, were you not upset, shocked, appalled, by an elected government being removed by force and a Serbian Crisis Staff taking power in Samac?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I object again. The witness has stated several times at which level he knew about the functioning of the government, and elections, now he's being asked about things that happened at municipal level. This should not be connected with his professional knowledge in order to talk about the veracity of this witness. He can be asked this as a citizen but the way this question is put indicates that he knew what the electoral procedure was and he's being asked whether he was shocked at the way that the government was changed at a higher level. He can be asked this as a citizen. And what he feels about it as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: This person has worked in the election process by his own testimony for 15 years. He was involved in the electoral rolls for 15 years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: At what level?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: At the local commune level. However, regardless of what level it's the local commune of Bosanski Samac which is the town of Samac which is 6.000 people which is the largest town in the municipality. Having worked for so long in the electoral process, he should be able to indicate his view or his feelings based on what happened which was basically an illegal takeover or a coup that occurred in Samac which is in direct violation of what he's been working on for 15 years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, but the point I'm making is that according to his evidence, and what he has stated here, he was involved in the elections at the local commune level. Not at the municipality level.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour it makes no difference what level. The fact that you've worked in a democratic system and helped put together a democratic system for many years would make you appalled by some dictatorship takeover and that's all I'm trying to get out, whether it's at a high level or lower level, any level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps as an individual citizen who was living in that area, who could have perhaps known what the events -- what events were taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And also having worked in an electoral process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Generally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, being a citizen of the area of Samac, being a member of the commune, local commune, having worked in the electoral process for 15 years, were you not shocked and appalled by what had happened in Samac, the electoral -- the elected government had been removed and a Crisis Staff had taken over the town of Samac?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: I can't answer this question. Firstly, because I didn't know what was happening, whether it was legal or illegal, and later on, when I found out what had happened, I simply accepted it as part of the entirety of what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So when you did find out, it didn't bother you that someone had taken over your town?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the witness has explained everything when he said he didn't know whether it was legal or illegal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. What he's doing is he's cluing the witness what to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. Let him finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm only repeating what the witness said. And now the witness is being asked to respond. The witness is not an expert. He's a fact expert -- he's a fact witness and he said what he thought, and now he's being asked again what he felt about the forcible takeover and he has already stated that he didn't know what -- that he can't answer that question, and now the Prosecutor is insisting on this again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, he indicated that he found out sometime later, so I'm asking him about sometime later when he found out, he said he accepted it, did it bother him? Did it upset him? Was he appalled by it? He can answer yes, he can answer no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: But he has said he accepted it so...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What does that mean? Did it bother him? I think it effects his credibility and I think it goes to his bias, especially when he joins the government after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Well go ahead and ask him, for whatever you think his answers will be worth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, when you then found out sometime later, and you joined the civil protection staff, did it bother you that the elected government was no longer in office and that a Crisis Staff had taken power?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it did bother me, but I accepted the facts as they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you remained there and you stayed in the civilian protection staff of the Samac municipality, of the Serb -- of the Serbian Municipality of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: The staff was not a Crisis Staff. It was a civilian protection staff at the Samac local commune, and it reflected the makeup of the population living in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the chief of that Crisis Staff was a member -- the chief of that civil protection staff was a member of the Crisis Staff, Miroslav Tadic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Whether Tadic was a member of the Crisis Staff, I don't know. I didn't go with him to sessions, nor did I read decisions. I only know that he was able to select a team of eminent citizens with whom he could work to assist the citizens, and that's what I was interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You were unaware that your supervisor was a member of the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Municipality of Samac? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: I think that to start with, he was not a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you aware, sir, that your supervisor was working with Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't aware that he was working with Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that your supervisor, Miroslav Tadic, was working with Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that your supervisor and chief of the civilian protection was working with Miroslav Tadic -- I'm sorry, was working with Stevan Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: No. I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you weren't aware of what he was doing, sir, isn't that correct? Outside of the civilian protection staff?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's time for our break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We will continue at 1100 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner? You can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning again, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And good morning, Mr. Volasevic.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You're welcome. Now, you indicated in your statement that you were a member of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you were issued a rifle by the 4th Detachment. Was that an automatic weapon?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you. It was a Russian weapon -- so I don't know whether it's automatic or semi-automatic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you trained in how to use that weapon, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And you also had another rifle, too, at your home?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: I had a trophy rifle at home from World War II that had the pin taken out of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was that the illegal weapon that you referred to in -- that you gave to the paramilitaries that were collecting weapons?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: This was not an illegal weapon because I had the proper paper work for that rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you state in paragraph 19 of your statement that you had an illegal weapon which you turned over to the paramilitaries indicating to them that that was your 4th Detachment weapon.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how long had you had that illegal weapon, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: For about 20 years, and it wasn't illegal. I had the proper paper work from the SUP about that, and they were the ones who took the pin out of the rifle and it was a trophy rifle from World War II.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement, you state -- you wrote, "I also had an old rifle which I held illegally." Is that incorrect or was this an illegal weapon? In your statement you indicated that were you holding an illegal weapon which you turned over to the Serb paramilitaries and indicated that was your weapon that you had received from the 4th Detachment. Was that the World War II rifle? Is that the illegal weapon? Or is that -- or did you have a third rifle?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't have a third rifle. That's the rifle that we are talking about. Maybe there is a misunderstanding in the terminology. Maybe as far as they were concerned that was a rifle that they didn't know I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, were you aware that Simo Zaric was interrogating residents of Samac concerning the possession of weapons, the possession of illegal weapons? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did Simo Zaric ever question or interrogate you concerning that rifle which you turned over to the paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't think he even knew that I had it. He didn't have any reason to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did Simo Zaric -- my question is did Simo Zaric ever question you, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did Simo Zaric ever contact you and set up an appointment for questioning? For you going to the police station and being questioned, concerning the possession of that rifle?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's continue on a few days later. On or about April 24th, in 1992, Miroslav Tadic comes to see you and says he's placing you on the civilian protection staff and you began working there, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were you aware that Miroslav Tadic also had other roles, that he was involved in exchanges?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You were not aware that Miroslav Tadic was involved in the exchange process?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: At the first moment, no, when we started to work with the civilian protection, but later I think I was in Samac when two exchanges were conducted, what -- who was exchanged and who participated in it, is not something that I could tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But did you at sometime learn that Miroslav Tadic was involved in the exchanges?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After about 20 days or a month, after the civilian protection headquarters began to operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. And did you also learn that Miroslav Tadic was involved in obtaining the release of the Serbian prisoners and residents of Odzak? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And Miroslav Tadic never told you or told you or the other members of the staff that he had attended any Crisis Staff meetings or that he had met with the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you were only aware of what Tadic was doing when he was with you at the civilian protection staff?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And he never indicated that Crisis Staff had ordered you, as members of the civilian protection staff, to do anything or that the -- or certain comments were being made by the Crisis Staff or that he had reported to the Crisis Staff, he had never discussed that with you, sir, any of those things?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Not with me personally, no, because I wasn't a member of the staff. I was a technical person there to provide assistance, to help them out. They had their own meetings, they had the meetings with the centre for social work, with the Red Cross, and I did not attend those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, while you're working in April, in May, of 1992, you were aware that non-Serb civilians were being arrested in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: I knew that they were arresting people but they were arresting Serbs too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How many Serbs were being arrested, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Specifically, I can recall two or three.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how many Muslims and -- I'm sorry, I'm going to strike that. Weren't hundreds of Muslims and Croats being arrested and being held at the TO building, the SUP building, the primary school building, the secondary school building?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: I heard that this was happening but I didn't have access there. I didn't see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And you heard that that was happening, were you also aware that Muslims and Croats were being isolated in such places as the high school and at Zasavica, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: I heard about some of them but there were many Muslims with me in the civilian protection, not all of them were taken away. I had Muslim neighbours as well so some were taken away but not all of them but I don't know on what basis they were being taken away. I think this is something that only the municipal authorities knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, had you heard the word "isolation" or isolated being mentioned in May and also in August -- May, June, July, August, in relation to some of these people?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure which people you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Some of these Muslims and Croats that were being held in Zasavica and the high school. Do you recall the term "isolation" or being isolated?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: I do but I couldn't really interpret it in its true sense because many people left Zasavica, they would come to my father's village, they would have lunch there, so they were free, and I think that isolation, that that term implies something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And at what period were they visiting your father's farm?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the exact date, and it wasn't at my father's house, but it was at my father's sister's house, Barjaktarevic would come there every day practically and spend a few hours there resting but I really cannot recall the exact period when this was happening in Zasavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, you indicated that prisoners, you were aware that prisoners were being held at various facilities. Did you or -- actually did the members of the civilian protection staff take any action to aid these non-Serb prisoners that were being mistreated at the SUP, meaning the police station, the Territorial Defence building, the primary school, or the high school?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
