utterances.text: I know that we were putting up glass on the elementary school windows because they were all shattered by the shelling. This was initiated by the civilian protection staff. It also launched an action to collect blankets so that we could take them to them so that they would have something to cover themselves with. Everything else was carried out by the municipal authorities. They didn't allow access there. The police was there so we would simply avoid those places.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you bring any medical supplies to this -- did the civilian protection staff bring medical supplies, bandages, underwear, sheets, pillows to any of those facilities? The police station, the Territorial Defence building, the primary school, the secondary school?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: According to what I know, I don't know, but I know that medicines were collected, all surplus that the citizens had and didn't need was collected in one place in town and anyone who needed such medicines would come to the civilian protection and we would send them to the emergency facility where all of these medicines were collected and then they would be given what they needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you don't know whether any of these medicines or any of the other goods, pillows, underwear, clothing, were sent to the prisoners, the non-Serb prisoners being held and mistreated at the police station, at the Territorial Defence building, the primary school or the high school? You don't know? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about it being organised, that's true, but there were a lot of individual cases of Serbs providing their friends with some food or cigarettes, things like that. This is something that I do know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And people were providing food to those non-Serb prisoners because they were starving at the Territorial Defence building, at the high school, at the secondary school and at the police station, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: We didn't know that, because we didn't have the opportunity to go inside and see what was going on. We didn't know, but we assumed, I myself took cigarettes to my friends with -- whether they had any or did not have any, in any case I did go and take some cigarettes for them just to have in case they wanted them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, when you say we don't know, you never discussed this matter with Miroslav Tadic so you can't answer as to his state of knowledge on whether or not the prisoners, the non-Serb prisoners, were starving at these prison camps or detention facilities?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't talk to Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that in a way, there is a trapping set for the witness because I do not wish to impute the answer but the witness couldn't find out about the conditions from Miroslav Tadic. I think this question is asking for a conclusion and it's being put in such a way to bring out an answer but it's actually also placing a trap for the witness. Perhaps it would be good to ask the question from whom did you hear about the conditions in prison? Was this something that was talked about in the town or no -- not?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's not my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: There is nothing wrong with the question Mr. Weiner has put to the witness and the witness can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the witness answered that he didn't talk to Mr. -- to the defendant Tadic about that. I didn't talk to Tadic was his answer to my question whether he had -- because he had indicated that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes the answer is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, in your statement, you talked about looting in Bosanski Samac, in paragraphs 26 and 28. You talked about stores were empty and were being looted and that other perishable goods were prone to looting. Now, sir, you were aware, you and members of the civilian protection staff were aware that stores and businesses in Samac were being looted, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: The terminology is not again quite -- there were stores where we had perishable goods, they were not broken into, but we had taken measures knowing that the goods would be spoiled but also at the same time we wanted to prevent anyone from breaking in at night. Mostly we would put away some derivatives, solvents, flammable oils, this is something that we removed because there was shelling several times a day so in order to prevent any consequences and in agreement with --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's not my question. My question is you were aware that stores in Bosanski Samac were being looted?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: No, they were not looted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, paragraph 26 of your statement, these stores were empty and were soon being looted. Nobody could protect them. My question again is, sir, you were aware in Bosanski Samac that stores or businesses were being looted.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were a couple of cases, but not all of them. Three or four shops perhaps and they were not completely looted, only the goods in the windows were taken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, weren't you aware of extensive looting in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know who Stevan Todorovic is, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Stevan Todorovic has pled guilty here and has admitted, and it's indicated in the sentencing judgement, the wanton and -- he's admitted to the wanton and extensive destruction, plundering and looting of the property of non-Serb civilians, including dwellings, businesses, personal property and livestock. You were not aware of the extensive looting in Bosanski Samac as a member of the civilian protection staff of that community?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: I told you about the local community in my previous answer but I don't know what happened in the wider area of the municipality so I don't know what the events were outside of my area of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you weren't aware of the extensive, organised looting campaign in Bosanski Samac of the non-Serb property? Throughout the municipality, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: There was no organised looting on a major scale, as far as I know, in the households in my town, but again I say I don't know what was happening at the level of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, in document which we are referring to is P127, is a document signed by one of the defendants, Simo Zaric, and it's from the military command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade. On page 4, it's just one, less than a sentence, it says the public looting of shops and private houses with the assistance of members of the military and civilian authorities, that's what it refers to, and a few pages later, on page 8, it indicates organised centres of power on both the municipal and broader republic level are behind organised looting. So you weren't aware of the organised looting throughout the municipality of Samac while you were a member of the civilian protection staff, were you, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The civilian protection staff, however, did discuss -- had to have discussed some part of this problem because they made a plan to inventory and remove these products from businesses throughout the town or -- isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness in the paragraph -- in paragraph 26, clearly explained the reasons why the property in the shops was inventoried, so it's clear from that what his knowledge was at that time about the extent of the looting. This is a task of the civilian protection where the witness explained why the commissions and the inventories were conducted and this is something -- and why the goods were removed. This has nothing to do with looting. He also explained which period this was done in. When the Prosecutor presented to the witness the document relating to Todorovic and document P127, these are the areas from 1992 and 1993, but this is something that was not told to the witness. The witness was only in Samac until September, 1992. So this needed to be explained to the witness, to specify the period about which the witness can provide a relevant answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, paragraph 28, other perishable goods or those prone to looting, were listed and then based on these lists, transferred to various depots. It's right in his statement. First sentence, paragraph 28.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it's there, yes. So you can go ahead with your questions. Mr. Lukic, the witness has stated what he knows in his statement, as well as in answer to the questions, so please let the Prosecution cross-examine unhindered. The witness will be able to answer what he knows and what he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand your decision, Your Honour, and this is why I explained it. The witness was not informed about the period, about which Mr. Todorovic and Mr. Zaric are testifying. This was not told to the witness. The judgement of Mr. Todorovic refers to 1992 and 1993 and talks about organised looting. The document of the 13 signatories was written in the fall of 1993, and it speaks about organised looting, and this was not stated by the Prosecutor but then he turns to ask the witness about organised looting in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've had a great deal of testimony here concerning organised looting, most of it has been uncontested in this Court. And it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Perhaps in fairness to the witness as Mr. Lukic it's better to be specific to the times when those other people consented or accepted or admitted that there was organised looting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, we've had testimony in this Court concerning looting, extensive organised looting, in the spring of 1992. You indicate that perishable goods prone to looting were inventoried and removed. Therefore, there had to have been some discussion before the civilian protection staff concerning looting in the spring of 1992, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Discussions were conducted more or less like this. There was an order to make an inventory, it was an instruction by the executive board, to inventory the goods, to certain goods, to be moved to a certain location, perishable goods to move to another location, so we acted upon those instructions. The other things were done by the organs of the police. They were the ones who dealt with instances of looting or whoever had broken into such facilities and so on. This is something that I didn't have any access to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It would have been done by the police unless the police and the Crisis Staff were involved in this organised looting, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: That I don't know. All I know is that it's their responsibility to prosecute the perpetrators. This is something that was not dealt with by the civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And had you ever heard of anyone ever being prosecuted in Bosanski Samac for looting, let alone murder of non-Serb civilians?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you said -- you put together an inventory of the various products in the stores and businesses and then these goods and services were all removed, placed on trucks, loaded on to trucks, unloaded off the trucks, placed in the warehouses. Although civilian protection staff was responsible for this, you didn't do the actual work of loading, unloading, storing, all of these goods? You didn't do that heavy lifting, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Didn't you or other members from the civilian protection staff go downstairs and visit Beg Kapetanovic and Dzevad Celic and ask for workers or labourers to do it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But only after this was approved by the Secretariat for national defence where we requested a certain number of people to help us bring in the goods as per the inventories. I wanted to ask that some of the members of the committee of the civilian protection who were there did help in these activities but it wasn't organised. We didn't all go there. I stayed in the office. Some of the people who were there to receive the goods and hand them over, they were the ones who helped out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, the people who did this work, those were the people who were lining up out in front of the local commune each day, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Not at the local commune but it was outside of the pensioners' hall where the Secretariat department was, the branch, the people were waiting outside of there and they were allocated to posts by the people from the Secretariat. We didn't have anything to do with them in our building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's correct. I'm sorry. Outside of the pensioners' home. And you knew those people, you recognised them, those were your Muslim and Croat neighbours that would be waiting out there each day?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a correction of the transcript. On page 53, in line 4, the witness said the Secretariat for national defence, but only the Secretariat has been mentioned in the record. We heard him say Secretariat for national defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: But I thought that's what it says. Line 3, line 4. It does say Secretariat for national defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes. Yes. I see, yes, further on it says Secretariat but it's clear what is referred to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And sir, you needed labourers for other jobs too, such as repairing glass, plumbing, electrical wiring?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you also needed labourers for all types of carpentry work, for repairs to windows, doors, roofs, walls, floors, in damaged buildings and houses?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you had to get materials to do this types of work, glass, wooden boards, doors, window frames, bricks, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the people who did all of this work wasn't your members of the civilian protection staff. Again, you were members of the civilian protection staff went to beg Kapetanovic, Dzevad Celic, and requested labourers?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: No. The number of labourers we needed, we asked the Secretariat for national defence for those. They would issue us with approval and then we would go to Dzevad to get the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you requested first to the Secretariat of national defence and then you went downstairs to Dzevad Celic and Beg Kapetanovic and got the authorised labour?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the people who did that work were those same individuals who were standing out in front of the pensioners' home each day waiting to do work?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic? Re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Volasevic.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Good day to you too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I haven't had an opportunity to address you yet. Now I will put a few questions to you which will help us to clarify certain points in the Prosecutor's questions, to clarify some points that the Prosecutor asked you about. I would only like to ask you to wait a little and make a pause after my question so that a question and answer don't overlap. The Prosecutor asked you today about the weapons issued to the local commune because of the duty roster. Who was it who issued the decision to set up a duty roster and to ask for weapons? Whose decision was it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: It was the council of the local commune extended with a coordinating body that was established a month or two previously in order to calm down the situation in the town, to set up mixed teams, to be on duty, in case anything should happen so that we could intervene on time, and on the basis of this, they decided to ask the Secretariat for weapons for their personal safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will not mention names because these are already in your written statement. I will just say that extended coordinating body or rather council, did it include members of all the parties, the political parties, in the Samac municipality who had representatives in the assembly of the Samac municipality? Do you remember whether this included members of the SDS, HDZ?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know but all the parties that won the elections HDS [as interpreted], HDZ, SDP, SDA and the reform forces, they all had representatives in the coordinating committee or the coordinating body, and they all nominated people to be on duty. Plus the local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the SDS too. It's not in the record.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were members of all the parties and representatives of the citizens part of these duty roster turns?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they all responded and they all took their turns.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were all ethnicities represented, both in the coordinating body and in the duty teams?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were never two people together from a single party. They were always from different parties and I myself made sure that this was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecutor asked you about the takeover of power, and the replacement of the legally elected government. You were asked whether this bothered you. I will ask you, were you bothered by the fact that there was war around Samac?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And did your family already take shelter somewhere?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you also whether you knew what the relationship was between Blagoje Simic and Miroslav Tadic and their participation in the government. While you were in the civilian protection staff, did you ever see Mr. Blagoje Simic visiting the civilian protection staff?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Tadic ever inform you what meetings he was attending, who was issuing decisions? Did he tell you about these things?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you now please look at paragraph 19 of your statement? The Prosecutor asked you about a rifle, whether Zaric questioned you about an illegal rifle, and you explained this word that's mentioned in your statement. You said in line 3 here to the special purpose member who asked you that you were a member of the 4th Detachment and that they had issued you with a rifle; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After that, the members of the special purpose unit said that regardless of the fact that you were a member of the 4th Detachment, you had to hand over the rifle to them?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And when you handed them this rifle, and said it was an old rifle, did you say that this was the rifle of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. He also asked you, the Prosecutor also asked you concerning your activities as a member of the civilian protection staff in connection with the detainees and you mentioned the blankets and the glass. Do you know that it was the Red Cross that was in charge of taking care of the detainees?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the local Red Cross took medicines and humanitarian aid to the detainees? Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor also asked you some questions in connection with the inventory of shops and goods and you said that a commission had been established and that you were in it. Do you know who formally issued the decision to establish a committee to seal the shops?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: It was the executive board of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it only civilian protection staff or others who were members of that commission?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was also citizens. For example, retired shop keepers who knew how to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who the President of the commission was for the inventory of the goods in the shops?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who the President was but I can tell you the names of the members, Ljubo Vukovic and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does the name Mihajlo Tolorovac [phoen] mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: It was Pero Tovjerac. Yes, I know the name. He was a retired shopkeeper. Unfortunately he died later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that he worked on the inventory?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was this man ever a member of the civilian protection staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I was just going to say the last one was leading, that's all. He was leading the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: This is redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'll allow it, Mr. Lukic. Please pause because you were overlapping with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question was: Do you know that this man worked -- or rather did this man work in the civilian protection staff while you were there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On making the inventories.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was he a member of the staff, the civilian protection staff?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you concerning the materials and the work that the civilian protection did in connection with buildings, glazing and the labour you needed for this. Do you know whether the civilian protection staff assisted members of all ethnic groups who applied to it for these repairs or was it only for a certain ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I never raised the issue of ethnicity of the people who were receiving any goods, services, it's outside the scope of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. It was contained in the answer so Mr. Lukic, Mr. Weiner is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I just have one small question, and it concerns what you mention in paragraph 28 of the statement, concerning the last couple of lines, last sentence, in fact, where you mention that if the owner of any of the stores returned, he'd get a copy of the record, presumably from the inventory that would have been made, so that he'd have a basis for requesting either return of his goods or compensation for them, and my query is just as to whether you have any knowledge as to whether this in fact occurred, if somebody returned to Samac, would that person or did that person, to your knowledge, if you know of any cases, get either goods returned or compensation in kind or monetary compensation?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Is that a question for me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. If you could.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I spent a very brief time in Samac. I know of no cases while I was there but what happened later, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO VOLASEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you for giving evidence. We are now finished. You may leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please make the solemn declaration. Please sit down. Has he made the solemn declaration? Oh, maybe my mike was not on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Who is examining this witness? Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before I begin, has the Chamber received the corrected statements of this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Have these been served on the Prosecution, these corrected statements?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think they are coming. I'm talking about the redacted statements, yes. Yes, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good day, sir. Can you tell us your first and last name?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Stojan Damjanovic, born on the 14th of February, 1933.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, your details have already been entered into the statement that is in front of you so you need not repeat them now. Mr. Damjanovic, just to clarify a point, in the statement you said you were retired. Were you retired before the 16th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: I retired in 1988.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you stated that you live in --

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Steve Obradovica street number 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please wait until I put my question and then pause for a few seconds to avoid overlapping? The two of us speak the same language but the interpreters need to interpret for all the other participants in the trial so in order for them to do their work properly, please wait until I finish my question and then pause for a few seconds to avoid overlapping. Have you seen this statement? Is this the statement that you signed in Samac? Mr. Damjanovic, tell me, in the previous paragraph, you said that you saw some men in front of your house at about 9.00 in the morning of the 17th of April. Among these men who were in the street in front of your house, did you see Miroslav Tadic?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us --

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him. I saw about ten men but I didn't know who they were, what sort of military they were, but I can assert with certainty that I didn't see Miroslav.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Damjanovic, could you please tell us how far is your house from the house of Miroslav Tadic?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: About 50 to 60 metres, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Damjanovic, when you saw those people, what did they look like? Were they local citizens from the Samac municipality or were they other people?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: They were not locals because they spoke with a Serbian accent, and I could hear that from my window. I could hear them talking. They were in multi-coloured uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see what those people were doing? Could you please describe it? Not that part about jumping over -- you already said that in your statement but tell us about the firing.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: There were two piles of bricks in front of my house, one of them fired a couple of bullets in the direction of Miro's or Miroslav's house. This other person commanded him not to shoot, then they searched the medical centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Just take it slowly, please, Mr. Damjanovic. I will ask you -- I will take you through it event by event but first finish this part about the shooting and then I will ask you the next question. So when you heard and saw this firing, did you see anyone on the balcony of Miroslav Tadic's house?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did. I saw Miroslav and I saw another man, they were waving with a white flag or a cloth. I don't know what because I really couldn't tell what it was. Then the soldiers started --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, could you please wait? We'll come to that. Did you hear if Miroslav Tadic was shouting something from the balcony?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Don't shoot, don't shoot.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Almost every question has been leading so far. It's not that difficult, surely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic, don't lead the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am trying to take the witness paragraph by paragraph so that he wouldn't just say -- tell things out of order but this is all I'm trying to do but I will try to stick to the instructions of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You can ask him what he saw, whom he saw, what he heard, when and where.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You saw that this man fired in the direction of Miroslav Tadic's house. At that point, when you saw and heard the shooting, did you hear whether Miroslav Tadic said something? Did you hear anything?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: I just said that. I heard, "Don't shoot, don't shoot." And he was waving. He said that in a loud voice but these people were in front of my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What else did you see? What did those people do after the firing?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: They went in the direction of the medical centre, they brought out the complete staff of the medical centre, they searched it. This is what they -- their instructions were, and then they went on, they moved on, so I didn't see them any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Damjanovic, could you please -- now I will give you a piece of paper so if you're able to, could you please sketch the position of your house and these facilities that you mentioned as well as the location of Miroslav Tadic's house so that we could get a clear picture of where you were and -- Mr. Damjanovic, to your right there is a pen and a piece of paper, so could you please sketch your street, draw your street, and your house, in the order that I ask you to. Please draw your street first and the location of your house.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please could you draw your house?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Just my house?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: For now, yes, just your house. One location by one location.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to your house, could you please draw the house of Miroslav Tadic?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Next to your house, could you please put the number 1?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And next to Miroslav Tadic's house, could you please put a number 2, mark it with a number 2?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Between your house and Miroslav Tadic's house, are there any other houses?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. There are no houses in between.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In this street, the street of D Obradovic, are there any houses next to yours?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please draw them? I'm talking about the other side, the side that is in the direction of Miroslav Tadic's house.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please move into private session? Because we are going to mention a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, can we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The sketch drawn by the witness, could it please be given an ID number and then we will have it translated because of the marking of the street? The witness has written on one of the houses, that it is Miroslav Tadic's house, so we would like to then, after it is translated, admit that, tender that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We will mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This sketch will be treated as document D186/3 ter ID.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Damjanovic, could you please tell us, did you see a tank that morning in your street?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Damjanovic, where did these people go afterwards?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: They went to the right, down a street that led to the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Damjanovic, could you please tell me, later, during that day, did you see Miroslav Tadic?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard him again up there on the balcony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when this was?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps at about 2.30 or 3.00, but I wasn't really paying attention to the time. I was just worried that the shells would kill us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Could you please tell us, those people in the camouflage uniforms, did they come back later?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did, and they were collecting weapons from the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Did they enter your house and did they ask you for weapons?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't. At that point, my son arrived from Pisari. He loaded us up into the car and took us over there because the shells had already started falling but my neighbours, also relatives, and my uncles houses, they took weapons from them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, the matters where you're supposed to lead the witness, are those contained in paragraphs 7 up to 11, and there is nothing about collection of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was about to stop the witness because all I wanted to ask is whether the men in the camouflage uniforms returned back and he started to reply but I was just about to stop him, to ask him to finish his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Damjanovic, I don't need to hear any more than that. All I was asking is whether those people had returned and whether later, when you were there, were there any -- was there a tank there during the time that you were there on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, there was no tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Cross-examination by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Damjanovic, I'm going to ask you some questions from the Prosecution, my name is David Re. Good morning. You're here to give evidence for the defendant, Mr. Miroslav Tadic?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You've known Mr. Tadic for a long time, haven't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: I've known him for perhaps 30 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: At the time, just before the war, he had a cafe called Cafe AS, were you a customer of his at Cafe AS?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you or have you been a member of a political party?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Never. Not even today. Other than the fact that I was a member of the League of Communists for a long time in the old Yugoslavia, during the time of Tito, but I was never a member of any other party, not during the war and not after the war either.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Although you say although you weren't a member of any political party, in the year before the war, that is 1991 to 1992, beginning of the war, I'm sorry, did you --

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you please wait until I finish my question, sir?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: During the period, the one year immediately before the war started in April, 1992, did you undertake any political activities, that is help a political party in any way? Campaigning, canvassing, attend meetings, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't, because I'm an invalid, I'm retired, I was looking after my grandchildren, I was looking after the house. I didn't attend any meetings. Nobody invited me to do so. I wasn't a military conscript. I wasn't a member of anything. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. When you said you have known Miroslav Tadic for 30 years, is he a friend of yours?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: What can I say? We saw one another infrequently. We didn't visit each other's homes and we didn't go out and sit in restaurants together either but we did know one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Would you consider yourself to be a long time acquaintance of Miroslav Tadic's?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, and that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Would you say that you had similar politics or political beliefs in 1992?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your political beliefs, you would have had some political beliefs in 1992. Do you know whether they were the same as Miroslav Tadic's?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know. I don't know what to tell you. I wasn't in any party. I wasn't called to go anywhere. So I can't really tell you anything in response to this question because I don't know anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Simo Zaric, another accused over there, you know him too, don't you?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. He was the director in the company where I worked for a long time, so I do know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You've known him for many, many years, is he a friend or an acquaintance of yours?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: An acquaintance. We are not -- we don't visit one another at home so he can only be an acquaintance.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about the third accused over there, Dr. Blagoje Simic? You know who he is too, don't you?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Dr. Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: I know him as well, but we are not family, we are not friends, we never sat down anywhere together.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said a moment ago you weren't a conscript. Do you mean by that that you weren't a member of the reserve of the JNA as of the first four months of 1992?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was neither a -- liable for military service nor was I a member of any military.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And in 1992, that is the first few months or at least leading up to the events of the 17th of April, were you aware of Mr. Tadic being a member of the JNA, the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't go out. I don't know who was where or who did what. I was never invited to any meetings, anywhere, for me to find out who was who and who was doing what.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said you were a customer of his cafe. You just said you didn't go out. You had to go out to go to his cafe, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Not during the war. I didn't go to cafes during the war. I didn't dare leave the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sir I was asking you about before the war, up to the 17th of April. I asked you about Mr. Tadic before the 17th of April. Can you please just cast your mind back to that? Were you aware in that period, in case there is any confusion, that Mr. Tadic was in the JNA, in the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you mobilised during the war?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you given a work obligation?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you given, after the 17th of April, 1992, a work obligation?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, nobody over 60 was given a work obligation and I was over 60 at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I thought you were born in 1933. That would have made you 59 in 1992, wouldn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm an invalid. Nobody made me work or do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In 1992, as of the 17th of April, did you own your house in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: I never left Samac. I did go down to the basement, fleeing from the shelling, but I never left my house. I can say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting. The witness is hard of hearing and is wearing a hearing aid. Perhaps the volume can be turned up. The witness often doesn't understand the question, which is the reason for the misunderstandings and the inappropriate replies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. Perhaps the hearing will now improve.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Damjanovic, can you hear me clearly? Can you hear the translation of what I'm saying clearly?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... it better than a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness nodded.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your nodding means yes?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sir, my question, what I want to ask you is about your house. Did you own it on the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you stay, did you remain in Samac, for the duration of the war?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you live there with your wife during the war?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: During the war, did other people such as refugees, come to stay in your house?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. We had two shelters. My house was not as well constructed so we went to those basements when there was shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm just asking you about people staying in your house during the war and of course you're still living there and you kept your house, no one took it from you during the war, did they, sir?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody stayed with me in my house. I was there, my wife, our daughter-in-law and two grandchildren. There are two rooms in the house, nobody could have stayed with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No one ever forced you to leave your house and go for an exchange somewhere, did they, sir?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No one did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was your wife at home with you on the morning of the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, she was. She was there. She was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your statement says that you heard shooting during the night, in the morning you saw someone's body, the body of someone you knew, and then you saw ten soldiers in camouflage uniform very close to your house and these people weren't locals.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I said in my statement and that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Given these things that happened, shooting, non-locals, armed, bodies in the street, you did what was -- you did what was -- you took precautionary measures and you stayed indoors, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. I didn't hear shooting in the night. I didn't say that. But in the morning, at 5.30, when this man was killed, who was brought to the health centre, his son fired a few shots there and his other son was a doctor in the health centre and he said they've killed my father. That's what it should say in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, having heard shots, seen a body, seen --

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see the body, because it was still dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So your statement says I saw that the body of Ilija Vukovic, a driver from Buducnost whom someone had shot had been transported to and placed outside the health centre?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Buducnost.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Hang on, hang on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, in fairness to the witness you should read the words before that. Because he does say sometime later when it got a bit lighter. Paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Maybe we are at complete cross-purposes here. I am only asking him about seeing a body. I don't really care when he saw it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, but in fairness it's better if you're quoting to quote what is before because it relates to what time he saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Certainly, sir, your statement says sometime later when it got a bit lighter I saw that the body of Ilija Vukovic, a driver from Buducnost, whom someone had shot had been transported to and placed outside the health centre located close to my house. All I'm asking you is -- that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. That's why I said I didn't see him being taken out but I saw him being put in the car and taken home, and it was already day light then.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. What I'm interested in is what you did afterwards. Not what happened before. Now, at that stage, there was a body -- you'd seen a body outside, heard shooting, seen soldiers with foreign accents very close to your house. You stayed indoors. Did you telephone anyone?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did I what?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you -- can you hear me clearly, sir?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: I can hear now. Could you repeat that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: After all those things had happened, did you telephone anyone to find out what was going on?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: No way.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was that because the telephones weren't working or because you didn't want to telephone anyone?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: There was no one I could have phoned. What would I say? We were all confused. There were attacks, there was shelling. I did have a telephone. It was operational but I didn't call anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said these people came to search your house for weapons. Did you own any weapons at that time? That is the 17th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say they came to search my house. I own a pistol, 765, and I've had it since 1974 but I never said they searched my house because when they came along collecting weapons I was already in my son's car, and the house was locked up.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do we take it from that that you kept your pistol because the soldiers didn't come into your house because you weren't there?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: I still have it. I've kept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The soldiers, as far as you know, came to your house to find out whether you had any weapons. That's from what you heard later, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: They couldn't have come because the house was locked up. When they were at my relatives, and my uncle's I was already in the car when they passed by my house. They didn't enter the house and they didn't search it. They couldn't have found it because I had it with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sir, did you not hear my question clearly? My question was coming to your house, not going into it. I'm just trying to establish clearly what you saw. Did you see soldiers come to your door and seeing there was no one -- knock on the door, no one answered it so they went away? Is that what you saw?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see that because there is a big iron gate in front of my house. I saw them coming out of other houses and going in the direction of my house but I was in the car already. They didn't search the car. And they were not able to enter the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: These soldiers you saw, were they -- the men in the camouflage uniform or local soldiers or a mixture?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Only camouflage uniforms. They -- their faces were painted as well. There were no local people there, not a single one. There were about ten of them. They were carrying weapons. And so they passed by.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: They didn't go into your house, you said you saw them go into some other houses. Did you actually see them go into the houses or just the yards?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Further on from my house, I didn't see anything because I left in the car. But up to my house, I've just said my uncle's house and my relatives' house they went into the yards, they collected the weapons, put the weapons on their backs and went on. Is that sufficient? Because that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What sort of artillery support did they have with them, these nine or ten soldiers in camouflage with blackened faces?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: How can I explain it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did you see? That's all I want to know. What did you see?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I saw about ten of them in camouflage uniforms with masked faces. I didn't see anything else. I saw them carrying rifles slung over their shoulders.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did these soldiers ever come back to your house when you returned to Samac several days later?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did any police ever come to your house, as far as you know, local police, looking for weapons?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When did you find out that there had been an ethnic takeover by Serb forces of Bosanski Samac, sir?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you say you don't know, is it that you can't remember?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's not that I can't remember. I really don't know. I told you I didn't attend any political meetings or rallies and I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sir, you said you left home on the 17th of April and came back maybe six days later. Were you aware by then when you came back that there had been a Serb takeover of the town you'd been living in for many years?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard all sorts of things but I didn't see that myself so I can't say anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's 12.30, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We will take our break and continue at 12.50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re. It's only about two, three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I only have that area to cover which is what happened on the morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, but you have to do it within your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Damjanovic, you at the moment you live on the name of the street you live on is Dositej Obradovic Street, correct, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was it formerly called Ulica Bulevar Revolucije Street; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And sir, you live between Djure Djakovica Ulica and Djure Putkara Sterok [phoen]; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Djure Djakovica Street is at right angles to my street but the other one, no, it's not between those two streets. Maybe there is this other street over there but I don't remember exactly. They changed the name several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sir, I just want to show you a diagram.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown, I have a blownup copy of D27/3. Please put that on the ELMO and have a look at it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sir, you recognise that as a map of Bosanski Samac with street names as they were in 1992, don't you? Sir? Mr. Damjanovic, can you hear my question?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I hear you. I know Samac, yes. Here near the stadium is where my house is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sir, my question is, you recognise that as a map of Samac with the old street names from 1992, that's all, please quickly look at it, agree with me and put it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't ask the questions in those two or three minutes. I just want him to mark on the map something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you have a pen there, sir? Please take the pen and put a little box on it in red and mark 1 where your house is, please. First, do you agree that the medical centre as marked on that map is between your house and Mr. Tadic's house, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now please mark with a 1 where your house is, draw a little square.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's the wrong street, sir. Look for Ulica Bulevar Revolucije. It runs from left to right through the middle of the map. That's the right street where your hand is.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You say by that can we see that your house is diagonally opposite the medical centre? Is that the position? Is your house on the same side of the street as the medical centre or diagonally opposite?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's in the direction. It's on the same line.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is it on the same side of the street, sir? That's all I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the same side, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Right. Can you see where medical centre is marked on that map, sir? Immediately to the left of the words "Ulica Bulevar Revolucije"? No, up, up, up, up, up. Move your hand up?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I assist perhaps by pointing it out to him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sir, just be quiet for a moment. You see Ulica Bulevar Revolucije? You see the medical centre there?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Medical centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Then I'm here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where my pen is.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: The stadium is not in front. I think my house should be here, and then the Tadic house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There is the SIT factory sir, you see? And there, just move your finger is Edvarda Kardelja Street, there, see? And your street goes there, that way, is your house there where my pen is?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Here. This is the stadium. This is my house. But it should be -- the street should be here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't hear Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe the witness cannot orient himself on the map and the point is what is the Prosecution contesting? Is it that his diagram not correct as to where he placed the things that he was asked to mark?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] The only diagram is incorrect --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The earlier diagram is incorrect according to other witnesses' evidence of where this witness's house is and where Mr. Tadic's house is, which impacts upon what he could have seen and the shooting. That's all I'm trying to get him to do is to put on the diagram which is in evidence where his house is and where Mr. Tadic's one is so that we can have a proper view of what he could have seen and where the soldiers were shooting from, according to the diagram which is already agreed to be a correct one and is in evidence. The diagram in evidence has the medical centre marked on it, it has the SIT factory marked on it, I just want him to put his house on it, Tadic's house on it, and the pile of bricks where he saw the soldier shooting from on it so we are all clear on the same diagram exactly where the witness was. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It depends on whether he can find his way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that this witness cannot orient himself on the map so there is no point in asking him this. When preparing him to draw the diagram, I explained to him how it can be done but perhaps the Prosecutor can ask him to describe the situation. I think that might be the better way.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: My learned friend introduced into evidence a diagram of this witness in which his house according to his own description, is in the wrong place. If the medical centre is to the left, the medical centre has to be between those two streets, Djure Djakovica and Edvarda Kardelja, which means his house has to be in the next block which takes it further away I'm -- we're talking about the line of fire towards Mr. Tadic's house and whether the shots were actually fired at Mr. Tadic's house or just in the direction of Mr. Tadic's house. And if it's on the diagram it would be obvious for everyone. I'm sure the witness who has already drawn a diagram if given and moment can see that the river is on the left, the school is on the right, his house must be facing one way because he lives there and has for many years. Maybe it might just take him a moment to orient himself but I'm sure he can do it. In my submission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. Let's see if he can do it. I'm sure he has had sometime to look at the map now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Damjanovic, are you now more familiar with this map?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the direction of the school, the street that is now called Dositej Obradovic street runs right next to the health centre. My house is on the same side as the health centre and the stadium is opposite. I cannot orient myself here but Miro's house is in the street which I think was called Djure Djakovica which runs towards the centre and it's at right angles to my house and I could see everything from my window in a diagonal line.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said your house is opposite the stadium. You can see the stadium there?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you please --

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. So I've drawn it here. Here is the stadium. Then my house, medical centre, then my house is here, if this is the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Then it's right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's not on the same side as the medical centre?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: About halfway down the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's not on the same side as the medical centre?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Yes, it is. It's on the same side as the medical centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But not as marked on the map. You're saying the medical centre is on the wrong place on the map?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: If it's marked and the street is also marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... M-e-d-i-c that's right there?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Medical centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There, there, yeah.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: And this is where my house is. Between the medical centre and me, there are two narrower houses and then there is the medical centre and Tadic's house is in the street leading straight to the centre of the town and I could see everything nicely from my window.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the Prosecutor tell the witness to mark the place where his house is?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, I want him to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Please, sir, could you please mark your house which you say is on the same side as the medical centre and opposite the stadium?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct, yes, then it's right here, that's how it comes out, if that's the medical centre then here is my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Please mark it on.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Please put a 1 in it and cross out the one down at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Know please mark on the map --

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: I have, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. With a 2, where Mr. Tadic's house was, or is.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: It should be here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Now, please mark with a 3 where you say the soldiers were behind the pile of bricks?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Here, in front of the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Please just mark with a 3 on the map, sir. That's all I want you to do.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The stadium is to your left, sir, you see where the word stadium is?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where you've marked is no where near the stadium, sir. It's near the school.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: But this is right next to my house. That's where I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, if that's where you saw it, just leave it there. Okay. You've now moved it, okay, can you please just write your name on this diagram on the top right, just please write --

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... in a white space, not in the photocopied bit but just in a white space, a clear space.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Here?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: What do you need -- should I put my phone number as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, the date is fine, 31 March 03, is fine. Just the date.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Might that be tendered into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have it marked, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it please be noted for the record that today is the 31st and could it be noted that today the witness made the markings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. It's dated the 31st, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's dated the 30th, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: He can correct it. It's supposed to be the 31st.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sir, you put yesterday's date on it. Could you please just write today's date?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Should I cross this out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sir, all you can say from those soldiers shooting is that they were shooting in the general direction of Mr. Tadic's house?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And when he called out, don't shoot me, did you hear him say something like don't shoot me, I'm a Serb, I'm a Serb?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. He didn't. He was just waving as I said with this white cloth and said, "Don't shoot" and then this man who was behind those other soldiers ordered them not to fire in that direction any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: They, like you, could see who the person on the balcony was. If you could recognise him they could also recognise the person if they knew him, couldn't they?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour, calling for speculation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And sir, after he called out don't shoot, the soldiers didn't go into his house, they went somewhere else, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: They went to the medical centre, to search it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of course the evidence you've given evidence is entirely from memory because you didn't make any notes at the time as to dates or the things you saw or times; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Damjanovic, I'm going to ask you a couple of questions. Do you remember well that day when war broke out in Bosanski Samac? This is not something that happens every day.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do I remember the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: The 17th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember those events that happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, all that I mentioned in the statement, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now I would like to ask you the following: Between your house and the house of Miroslav Tadic, are there any buildings which would block your view or is that a clear space?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. There are no buildings. It's a clear space.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And now just one small detail in your description to the Prosecutor when he asked you about these people, about the search of weapons and who had the weapons confiscated from them. What was the ethnicity of your neighbours whose weapons were confiscated?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if I can say it freely, they were Serbs, Orthodox Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object to this. I did not ask him that. I asked him about -- he told us about his uncle and a relative, I didn't ask him about neighbours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic, that wasn't raised, the ethnicity of his neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am asking him about these people. They are his neighbours and his relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your relatives who had the weapons confiscated and whom you mentioned in your reply to the Prosecutor, were they Serbs?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Radovan and Nenad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know their last names?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Their last names? Yes, yes, of course, they are both called Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the Prosecutor showed you the map and the Dositej Obradovic Street. What is the neighbourhood that you live in called?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: The 3rd neighbourhood. That was the name of it. Unless something has changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So it's not the 4th, is it? What about the area where Miroslav Tadic's house is? What is the name of that neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I don't think the map has been tendered into evidence yet, Your Honour, or given a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I thought the Registry assistant was still searching for the number. Can we have the number please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'm afraid I was given to chance. This map will be treated as Exhibit P171. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Damjanovic, I just have two questions for you. I presume you can hear me. You can hear me?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you. The first question relates to paragraph 12 in your statement, where you state that later in the day, on the 17th of April, 1992, your son came from the village of Pisari and took you with him to Pisari where you stayed for a few days. Now, I am just wondering when you left by car with your son, you've told us this afternoon that you had your pistol with you at that time. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay. What I want to know is, on the trip from town in Samac to Pisari, were you stopped at any checkpoints by soldiers of some description?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's the first question. The second question relates to something that the Prosecutor asked you concerning whether you had any work duty or work obligation during the war, after April 17th, 1992. And you said no. What I'd like to know is: Did other members of your family have work obligation? For example your wife, your son, your daughter-in-law?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DAMJANOVIC
utterances.text: The wife did not. My daughter-in-law went with my son. My son had to go to Germany. He was there for medical treatment so she went with him and that's where they stayed.
